newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FASB board may opt for new derivatives plan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FASB board may opt for new derivatives plan.

text.p: The Financial Accounting Standards Board, the independent group that sets industry reporting standards, may opt to release a new proposal rather than final rules for companies to abide by when they use complex financial instruments, an official said Thursday.

FASB's director of research, Timothy Lucas, on Thursday told a group of derivatives professionals at a conference the drafting process continues to be tedious and the accounting board may have to issue a new proposal on June 30.
"I believe it is reasonably possible that the board will choose to re-expose (circulate a formal proposal)," he said.
Such a move could delay approval of the controversial derivatives hedge accounting rules for several months and possibly years.

And the delay is not likely to be good news to Securities and Exchange Commission chairman Arthur Levitt, who last December urged the accounting board to "bring an end to this process." At that time the board promised to finish the project by June 30, before its next board election.
Lucas said that if the board decides to issue a new draft, a review would not likely be finished before the second quarter of 1998.
"It just takes us nine months or a year to go a lap around this track every time. This is not a simple document and if we do re-expose we will re-deliberate everything again," he said.
Lucas defended the potential delay in completing the new accounting standards.
"For very good reasons, and everybody agrees, our process of having an exposure before we have a final is appropriate. So nobody to my knowledge is suggesting that we shouldn't do that."
Efforts to design the special accounting rules began more than three years ago because regulators and some accounting professionals felt these activities were not adequately reported.

Industry professionals, including the International Swaps and Derivatives Association, have faulted the accounting effort, saying the plan would lead to volatile financial reporting and ultimately drive companies from using derivatives.
